title: Type 1 diabetes, hypoglycaemia and DKA in children
blurb: Spot new type 1 diabetes and refer the same day, treat hypoglycaemia by severity, and nurse a child with DKA safely using NICE NG18 and the BSPED guideline.
question: Amir, 13, has vomiting, abdominal pain and deep sighing breathing. His glucose is 28 mmol/L, venous pH 7.15 and blood ketones 5.4 mmol/L. How severe is his DKA, and when should his insulin infusion start?

teach.body: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas stops making insulin. Children classically present with thirst, passing lots of urine (including new bedwetting), weight loss and tiredness. Without insulin the body burns fat, making ketones, and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) follows. Plain English: a thirsty, weeing, thinning child needs a same-day glucose check and, if suspected, same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team.

head: Item
Target or standard
rows: Glucose on waking and before meals
48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower; checked 4 times a year
Basal-bolus injections or pump; carbohydrate counting
teach.caption: Every family also needs blood ketone strips, sick-day rules and an annual flu vaccine from 6 months.

steps.label: Then
steps.sub: Complex carbohydrate, unless a meal is due or on a pump

steps.label: Severe, cannot swallow
steps.sub: IM glucagon; buccal gel only if conscious

teach.caption: Glucagon: 1 mg if over 8 years or 25 kg or more; 500 micrograms if under 8 years or under 25 kg. In hospital, IV glucose is used.

letters.word: Acidosis: pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15

head: Severity
Venous pH (or bicarbonate)
Assumed deficit
teach.caption: Children with known diabetes can develop DKA with near-normal glucose, so check ketones when they are unwell.

steps.label: Shocked?
steps.sub: 10 mL/kg 0.9% NaCl over 15 min, repeat to 40 mL/kg

steps.label: Insulin infusion
steps.sub: 1–2 h after starting IV fluids; 0.05–0.1 units/kg/h; no bolus

steps.label: Glucose at 14
steps.sub: Add glucose to the IV fluids

teach.caption: Potassium is added once the child is passing urine or potassium is within normal range. If potassium is below 3.0, defer insulin. Stop an insulin pump when IV insulin starts.

teach.body: Keep strict fluid balance. Check capillary glucose hourly and blood ketones every 1 to 2 hours, with hourly BP and observations. Record level of consciousness hourly using the modified GCS, or half-hourly with heart rate for children under 2 and those with pH below 7.1, who have a higher risk of cerebral oedema. Report headache, slowing pulse or any change in consciousness or behaviour to the doctor immediately, even at night.

teach.text: Cerebral oedema in DKA often appears hours into treatment, when the child seems to be improving. Headache, irritability, a slowing pulse, rising BP or a falling conscious level are not 'just tiredness': treat immediately with hypertonic saline or mannitol and get senior help.

teach.h: Scenario: Ruby, 6, at the GP surgery
teach.body: Ruby has lost weight over three weeks, is drinking constantly and has started wetting the bed again. Her capillary glucose is 19 mmol/L. Practice nurse Sian does not arrange a fasting test or a routine HbA1c. She tells the GP, who phones the paediatric diabetes team and arranges for Ruby to be seen the same day, because delay risks DKA.

items: Suspected type 1 diabetes: same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team.
Hypo: 10–20 g fast glucose, recheck at 15 min; glucagon 1 mg (over 8 years or 25 kg+) or 500 micrograms.
DKA: glucose usually over 11, pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 15, ketones over 3.
Fluids first; insulin 1–2 h later at 0.05–0.1 units/kg/h, no bolus; deficit over 48 h.
Watch for cerebral oedema: headache, slowing pulse, rising BP, falling consciousness.

summary: You can now recognise new type 1 diabetes and refer the same day, treat hypoglycaemia by severity, and diagnose and grade DKA. You can also follow the BSPED order of fluids then insulin, monitor closely and act on signs of cerebral oedema.

A.q: Amir, 13, has vomiting, abdominal pain and deep sighing breathing. Glucose 28 mmol/L, venous pH 7.15, ketones 5.4 mmol/L. How severe is his DKA?
A.why: BSPED: venous pH 7.1 to 7.19 is moderate DKA (assume 5% dehydration).

whyNot.3: Ketones over 3 with pH under 7.3 and glucose over 11 meet the DKA criteria, not those of HHS.

A.q: Ruby, 6, has lost weight, is drinking constantly and is wetting the bed again. Her capillary glucose is 19 mmol/L. What should happen?
options: Book a fasting glucose next week
Start metformin and review in clinic
Repeat the glucose level in a month
A.why: NG18: refer children and young people with suspected type 1 diabetes the same day to a multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team.

whyNot.1: Metformin is not the treatment for suspected type 1 diabetes.

A.q: Jake, 10, has type 1 diabetes. In the school nurse's office he is shaky and sweaty, and his glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. He is alert and can swallow. What should the nurse give?
options: Wait and recheck his glucose in 30 minutes
A.why: NG18: treat mild or moderate hypoglycaemia with 10 to 20 g of oral fast-acting glucose, then recheck within 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: Glucagon is for severe hypoglycaemia when the child cannot take oral glucose.
whyNot.2: Complex carbohydrate follows fast-acting glucose; it acts too slowly first.
whyNot.3: Hypoglycaemia needs treatment now; waiting 30 minutes lets it worsen.

B.q: After 15 g of glucose tablets for a hypo, Kiran, 12, is rechecked at 15 minutes. His glucose is now 5.2 mmol/L and lunch is not due for 2 hours. He uses injections. What next?
options: Recheck in 1 hour with no food
B.why: Once glucose has recovered, give some complex (longer-acting) carbohydrate unless a meal is due or the child uses a pump.

whyNot.1: Further fast glucose is for a level that is still low.
whyNot.3: Without complex carbohydrate the glucose may fall again.

B.q: Lola, 6, weighs 21 kg and has type 1 diabetes. At home she is drowsy and cannot swallow safely; her glucose is 2.0 mmol/L. What glucagon dose should be given?
B.why: NG18: glucagon 500 micrograms for children under 8 years or under 25 kg; 1 mg if over 8 years, or 25 kg or more.

whyNot.0: 1 mg is for children over 8 years old, or weighing 25 kg or more.
whyNot.1: 250 micrograms is below the recommended dose.
whyNot.2: 2 mg is above any NG18 dose.

B.q: Ella, 9, has moderate DKA and is not shocked. She has had a 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 minutes. When should the IV insulin infusion start?
B.why: BSPED: start the insulin infusion 1 to 2 hours after beginning IV fluid therapy, at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, with no bolus.

whyNot.0: An insulin bolus is not given in children with DKA.
whyNot.1: Fluids come first; insulin is started 1 to 2 hours later.
whyNot.3: Insulin is what clears the ketones, so it cannot wait for them to fall.

C.q: Noah, 7, is 6 hours into treatment for severe DKA. He was alert on admission. He now complains of headache, is irritable, and his heart rate has dropped from 120 to 80 while BP has risen. What should the nurse do?
C.why: Headache, irritability, slowing pulse and rising BP are BSPED warning signs of cerebral oedema; it needs immediate treatment and senior help.

whyNot.0: Treating the headache alone misses a life-threatening complication.
whyNot.1: Waiting an hour delays urgent treatment.
whyNot.2: More fluid may worsen cerebral oedema.

C.q: Freddie, 18 months, has severe DKA with a pH of 7.02. How often should his neurological observations be recorded?
C.why: BSPED: half-hourly neurological observations (modified GCS and heart rate) for children under 2 or with pH below 7.1, due to higher cerebral oedema risk.

whyNot.0: 4-hourly is far too infrequent in DKA.
whyNot.2: Hourly is the standard for lower-risk children; he is under 2 with pH under 7.1.
whyNot.3: 2-hourly misses early signs of cerebral oedema.

C.q: Sophie, 14, uses an insulin pump and is admitted in DKA. IV insulin is about to start. What should happen to her pump?
options: Stop it when IV insulin starts
Continue it at the usual basal rate
C.why: BSPED: for children on continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion, stop the pump when starting intravenous insulin.

whyNot.1: Running both risks excess insulin; BSPED stops the pump.
whyNot.2: Doubling the pump rate is not part of DKA management.
whyNot.3: No insulin bolus is given in paediatric DKA.

reteach.title: Water first, insulin second, watch the brain
reteach.question: Why does a child with DKA get fluids before insulin, and why do nurses watch so closely?

blocks.body: A child in DKA is dry and acidotic. BSPED replaces fluid carefully over 48 hours and starts insulin 1 to 2 hours after the fluids, without a bolus. Careful fluid management matters because of the risk of cerebral oedema, which is more common in younger children and new diagnoses. So nurses check glucose hourly, ketones every 1 to 2 hours, and consciousness closely.

blocks.text: Glucose falling to 14 is not the end of DKA. Keep the insulin running to clear the ketones, and add glucose to the fluids instead.

explain.body: Thirst, polyuria, bedwetting, weight loss and tiredness suggest type 1 diabetes: same-day referral. NG18 targets: 4–7 before meals, 5–9 after, HbA1c 48 or lower.

test.q: What HbA1c target does NG18 set for children with type 1 diabetes?
test.why: NG18: an HbA1c target of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower.

whyNot.3: 42 mmol/mol is not the NG18 figure; the target is 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower.

explain.body: Mild or moderate: 10–20 g fast glucose, recheck within 15 minutes, then complex carbohydrate. Severe out of hospital: IM glucagon 1 mg (over 8 years or 25 kg+) or 500 micrograms.

test.q: How soon should glucose be rechecked after treating a mild hypo?
test.why: NG18: recheck within 15 minutes and repeat treatment if still low.

whyNot.0: 2 to 5 minutes is too soon for oral glucose to act.
whyNot.2: An hour leaves a persisting hypo untreated.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a meal is too long.

explain.body: Shocked: 10 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat to 40 mL/kg. Not shocked: 10 mL/kg over 30 min. Deficit over 48 h plus maintenance. Insulin 1–2 h after fluids, 0.05–0.1 units/kg/h, no bolus.

test.q: Over what period is the DKA fluid deficit replaced in the BSPED guideline?
test.why: BSPED: replace the deficit evenly over 48 hours, plus maintenance.

whyNot.0: 12 hours is too rapid and risks cerebral oedema.
whyNot.1: 24 hours is faster than BSPED advises.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is longer than BSPED advises.

explain.body: Strict fluid balance; hourly glucose; ketones every 1–2 hours; hourly obs and GCS; half-hourly neuro obs under 2 years or pH below 7.1. Report headache, slowing pulse, behaviour change at once.

test.q: How often should capillary blood ketones be checked in a child with DKA?
test.why: BSPED: capillary blood ketones every 1 to 2 hours.

whyNot.2: Twice daily is far too infrequent.
whyNot.3: Ketones must be monitored throughout treatment.
